name: Dry mouth management (Biotene)
lead: Dry mouth management refers to products and habits used to relieve xerostomia, the sensation of a dry mouth, including saliva substitutes in the form of sprays, gels, rinses and lozenges. Biotene is a widely sold brand of such products.[1]

Dry mouth matters to dental appearance communities because lack of saliva, which buffers acid, is linked to rampant tooth decay, mouth soreness, candida infection and intraoral bad breath.[1] Wikipedia reports that no topical therapy has strong evidence of effectiveness and that benefits are generally short-term.[1]

People use these products mainly to keep the mouth moist and comfortable, and through that to protect the teeth, gums and breath that shape how a smile looks and how close conversation feels. Biotene sells sprays, gels, rinses, toothpastes and lozenges in this category; its published trials are mostly small, short crossover or pilot studies in people with measured low saliva flow, including patients after head and neck radiotherapy [6][7][8].
infobox: Roughly 20 percent of the general population, higher in older adults [1]
Medicines (over 400 linked), Sjogren syndrome, head and neck radiotherapy, mouth breathing, dehydration [1]

paras: Over 400 medicines are linked to dry mouth, and other causes include Sjogren syndrome, head and neck radiotherapy, mouth breathing and dehydration.[1] Effects include caries, mucosal soreness, candidiasis and halitosis.[1]

Wikipedia describes xerostomia as the subjective sensation of dryness, which often but not always accompanies reduced salivary flow. Its summary puts prevalence at around 20 percent of the general population, up to about 30 percent of women and up to about 50 percent of older adults [1]. Because saliva buffers acids, its absence is associated with fast decay at unusual sites such as root surfaces, acid erosion, candidiasis, altered taste, burning sensations, sticky saliva, and difficulty chewing, swallowing or wearing dentures [1]. Intraoral halitosis is attributed in the same article to bacterial biofilm at the back of the tongue, and a perceived bad breath can also arise from taste disturbance without true hyposalivation [1]. Medicines are the most common cause, including antidepressants, opioids, antipsychotics, antihypertensives and diuretics, and the risk rises with the number of drugs taken [1]. Head and neck radiotherapy that reaches the salivary glands can cause severe dysfunction [1].

Saliva substitutes coat the mouth and give temporary relief; Grokipedia notes no specific trials are cited for them.[2] Wikipedia notes mucin sprays have no strong evidence of beating placebo, and a 1999 trial (Epstein) found Biotene more effective than control and reduced dryness on waking.[1] Some acidic moisturisers below about pH 6.7 may pose a risk to root dentine.[1]

Wikipedia's product-level summary lists several results. Biotene Oral Balance gel and toothpaste were more effective than control in the 1999 Epstein crossover trial, which found reduced dryness on waking [1][8]. Four trials of mucin sprays found no strong evidence they beat placebo, one trial with high risk of bias found mucin lozenges no better than placebo, and a trial of mucoadhesive palate disks reported that both active and placebo disks improved subjective moistness [1]. The article also advises sugar-free products, because sugars feed acid-producing bacteria, and notes that some moisturisers below about pH 6.7 may risk root dentine depending on formulation [1].

Management begins with addressing the cause where possible, such as reviewing medicines or treating dehydration and mouth breathing [1]. Saliva stimulants are also used: pilocarpine may help when some gland function remains, though evidence is mixed and improvement can take weeks; sugar-free gum and xylitol increase saliva flow without strong evidence of symptom relief; and amifostine has low-quality evidence for reducing radiation-related dryness [1]. A 2003 clinical review in Gerodontology similarly notes that dry mouth is common in older people, who are more often on multiple medications [10].

A 2025 umbrella review of 48 systematic reviews found only three high-quality reviews. It reported that limited evidence suggests topical therapies offer palliative or stimulating effects on symptoms, and low-quality evidence indicates a slight increase in saliva with acupuncture [4].

sections.h: How dry mouth affects teeth, breath and appearance
paras: The US National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research explains that saliva carries calcium and phosphate that help keep teeth strong and counter decay, so reduced flow raises the risk of tooth decay and fungal infections in the mouth [11]. The same page lists medicines for high blood pressure, depression and bladder problems, conditions such as Sjogren's disease and diabetes, head and neck radiation, and nerve damage among common causes, and states that dry mouth is not a normal part of aging [11].

For people who care about how their smile and breath come across, this is the link: a moist mouth is the starting point for keeping enamel intact, tongue coating and breath in check and lips and gums comfortable. Saliva substitutes are one tool in that chain; they do not cure the underlying cause, and clinicians commonly pair them with a review of medicines and with dental check-ups [1][11].

Over-the-counter dry mouth products come as sprays, gels, rinses, toothpastes and lozenges. A 2003 review in Supportive Care in Cancer describes lubricating mouthwashes and gels as options for painful, damaged oral mucosa, notes that a mild-tasting children's toothpaste may suit people for whom regular toothpaste tastes too strong, and says nocturnal dryness can be eased by spraying the mouth [12]. The same review lists mechanical or gustatory stimulation and cholinergic drugs such as pilocarpine or cevimeline for people with remaining gland function [12].

NIDCR's self-care list includes sipping water through the day and with meals, limiting caffeine, avoiding tobacco and alcohol, using a bedside humidifier, and chewing sugarless gum or sucking sugarless candy to stimulate saliva; it adds that some xylitol-containing gums may help prevent cavities [11].

Biotene is an over-the-counter oral-care brand now marketed by Haleon and previously sold by GSK, with toothpaste, mouthwash, spray and gel products [16]. Wikipedia reports that earlier formulations contained the enzymes glucose oxidase, lactoperoxidase and lysozyme, plus lactoferrin, and that the formulation changed after the GSK acquisition; the article's toothpaste active is sodium monofluorophosphate [16]. The same page says Biotene works by moisturising rather than by preventing plaque or acting as an antimicrobial [16].
Wikipedia's coverage of the brand carries maintenance notes about promotional tone and sourcing, so brand-specific claims there are best read alongside the trial literature summarised below [16].

sections.h: Dry mouth, breath and the tongue
paras: Bad breath is among the main appearance-adjacent reasons people look for dry-mouth care. Wikipedia reports that roughly 85 to 90 percent of genuine halitosis cases start in the mouth, mostly from odour-producing bacterial biofilm on the back of the tongue, and that some medications cause dry mouth that lets microbes grow more easily [17]. The same article notes that alcohol-containing mouthwashes can dry the mouth and may worsen odour, and that tongue cleaning, brushing, flossing and treating gum disease and cavities are the initial measures, with no single intervention shown to be the most effective [17].

Proponents of saliva substitutes describe them as a comfort and moisture tool that sits alongside these measures. Clinicians quoted in the reviews tie the underlying cause, often medication, to the problem and treat the substitute as symptom relief [1][10].

A multicentre randomised 28-day trial compared an experimental oral gel, a commercial rinse and a mouth spray with water for self-reported dry mouth symptoms and quality of life.[3] A 2025 umbrella review of systematic reviews examined management of xerostomia and hyposalivation,[4] and a 2021 review discussed strategies including electrostimulation.[5] Wikipedia notes a 2013 review found no evidence supporting electrostimulation or acupuncture.[1]

Biotene-specific studies are mostly small. A double-blind, randomised crossover trial in 2021 compared a single dose of Biotene Moisturizing Spray with water spray for how long relief lasted, enrolling adults whose unstimulated saliva flow was at or below 0.20 mL/min [6]. A double-blind crossover study in post-radiotherapy patients compared Biotene Oralbalance with the BioXtra system as saliva substitutes [7], and the 1999 Epstein trial compared Oral Balance gel and Biotene toothpaste with placebo in patients with xerostomia after radiation [8]. A pilot study compared a mucoadhesive lipid-based tablet with Biotene mouthwash for dry-mouth relief [9].

A 2026 review of Phase III and IV trials registered in cancer-care settings reported that pilocarpine, amifostine and cevimeline significantly improved salivary function in radiotherapy-induced xerostomia, and that Phase IV studies supported Biotene, among other products, for symptom relief and comfort, while noting wide differences in study design [13]. A randomised crossover trial in laryngectomy patients with voice prostheses compared nystatin with Biotene mouthwash for controlling Candida, framed around Biotene as a lower-cost alternative that needs less contact time [14].

Reviews of Biotene's wider claims report mixed findings outside dry-mouth symptoms: Wikipedia cites a 1997 study in which Biotene alone did not significantly reduce Streptococcus mutans, and a 2015 crossover trial in which a chlorhexidine rinse prevented plaque regrowth better than Biotene [16].

card.summary: Saliva substitutes like Biotene give short-term dry-mouth relief; no topical therapy has strong evidence.
card.note: Acidic products below about pH 6.7 may risk root dentine.

quick.overview:
Dry mouth products such as Biotene are sprays, gels and rinses that coat the mouth to relieve dryness, used because lack of saliva raises risks of decay and bad breath.

Research summaries say none has strong evidence and benefits are short-term.
quick.mechanism: They lubricate and coat the mouth, imitating some of saliva's function; they do not restore salivary flow.
quick.risks: Products are generally low risk, though some acidic moisturisers may harm dentine, and sugar-containing ones may feed decay bacteria.

chain: Saliva substitute coats and moistens the mouth
Dry-mouth discomfort and overnight dryness ease
Less dry-mouth halitosis and decay pressure on the teeth
Fresher breath and a healthier-looking smile
angle.text: People with a dry mouth use sprays, gels and rinses such as Biotene to lubricate the mouth, usually before bed or during the day. Because saliva buffers acid and washes bacteria from the teeth and tongue, keeping the mouth moist is the first step in the chain toward fresher breath and less decay-related damage to teeth.
